header:
Date: 2026-01-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Maven - Head of Security), Daniel Ortiz (Maven - Platform), Marta Silva (Maven - Privacy Counsel), Rory Nguyen (Maven - SRE)
summary: Customer wanted deep dive on region pinning, cross-border processing risk, subprocessor list, and KMS integration options (customer-managed vs Redwood-managed). Clarified Redwood's hosted, dedicated, and private behaviors for data residency. Agreed next steps to exchange attestation artifacts and schedule KMS integration session.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick agenda — region affinity, our subprocessor map, and KMS options. Uh Priya and Ethan will jump into technical bits.
[00:12] Aisha: Thanks Jordan, quick context — we are onboarding a set of inference-powered features for patient triage, so data residency is critical. We need to be sure PHI doesn't leave EU when the user is in EU.
[00:26] Priya: Great, yeah, that's the right place to start. Quick note — we'll cover three modes: hosted, dedicated, and private. Each has different guarantees.
[00:38] Daniel: Quick question, sorry, hosted means Redwood's public cloud endpoints, right? So data might route to US?
[00:46] Priya: Correct, hosted by default is multi-region with smart routing; we can do region affinity to prefer EU, but default hosted isn't guaranteed for strict sovereignty. For full residency you want Dedicated in-region or our Private VPC/on-prem offering.
[01:02] Marta: And Dedicated truly pins processing to a region/GCP or AWS region? We need contractual guarantees for some contracts.
[01:10] Ethan: For Dedicated we map customer capacity to specific cloud region(s). So compute and KV caches stay in that region. There's still minimal control plane traffic for metrics and billing unless you select Private where the control plane is customer-facing. There is a small nuance around metadata and audit logs — we can route logs to your S3/GCS in-region or forward to your SIEM via private peering.
[01:34] Aisha: Okay, can you explain the control plane traffic you mentioned? Even metadata like request id could be considered personal data by our privacy team.
[01:44] Priya: Totally — Redwood's control plane handles orchestration and metadata. For Dedicated we can minimize it and encrypt in transit. For Private we can offer a customer-controlled control plane (VPC endpoint) so metadata never leaves. We'll follow up with exact fields we consider metadata.
[01:58] Rory: If we go Dedicated in eu-west-1, what about sub-processors? Are any of your infra subprocessors US-based and could they access data?
[02:06] Jordan: Good callout. We maintain an up-to-date subprocessor inventory — most compute infra is major cloud providers (AWS/GCP) in region, but some tooling like our analytics (Housekeep) and monitoring may be US-based. We'll share a CSV with locations and contractual controls.
[02:24] Marta: We need SOC 2 and ISO docs and explicit subprocessor locations to present to legal.
[02:30] Priya: We'll attach SOC 2 Type II, our ISO 27001 certificate, and the subprocessor list. Note, subprocessors that handle telemetry can be restricted in Dedicated/Private deployments.
[02:40] Aisha: Another angle — encryption at rest and KMS. We need customer-managed keys (CMK) in our AWS account if possible. How does Redwood support CMKs?
[02:50] Ethan: We support several modes: Redwood-managed keys, customer-managed KMS via key share, and a Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) flow. For Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS, using key policies and grant patterns so Redwood worker roles can use the key without having key material. For Private, full BYOK is possible with HSMs.
[03:10] Daniel: When you say integrate with our KMS, does that mean tokens or temporary grants? We want no key material to be transferred.
[03:18] Priya: We never take key material. For AWS KMS we use IAM role grants and generate data keys in your account; Redwood services get only the ciphertext. For GCP KMS similar patterns exist. We can also do KMS proxying through a customer network in Private mode.
[03:36] Marta: Is there a latency impact? Our SLOs are tight.
[03:41] Ethan: There's a small added RTT for KMS calls — usually sub-10ms if in-region. For high-throughput inference we recommend envelope encryption with cache of plaintext data keys that are rotated and rewrapped, to keep token latency acceptable. We can provide benchmarks.
[03:58] Aisha: Benchmarks would be great. We have a latency SLO of 150ms p95 for interactive triage flows.
[04:06] Priya: Understood — we'll include sample latency numbers with KMS integration and quantized model variants. Also we can recommend batching/caching settings to meet 150ms p95.
[04:18] Rory: About cross-border fallbacks — if eu-west-1 is saturated, will Redwood route to us-east-1 and process EU data in US? That's a dealbreaker for us.
[04:28] Jordan: By default, routing policies allow fallback but it's configurable per-customer. We offer 'strict region pinning' which returns 429s instead of failing over to other regions. For Dedicated you can set strict pinning. For hosted we can set preference but it's not hardstops unless we add policy enforcement in the DPA.
[04:46] Daniel: So we should push for Dedicated then for strict compliance, correct?
[04:50] Priya: Yes, Dedicated or Private are the safe bets. Dedicated provides strong in-region guarantees; Private gives the most control (customer-run control plane).
[04:58] Marta: On the DPA — can you add contractual language that you won't fallback cross-border without explicit approval?
[05:04] Jordan: We can include region pinning obligations and a clause that requires customer approval for cross-border processing, and we can tie it to SLAs. I'll send a redline.
[05:14] Aisha: Audit logs — we need immutable audit trails for who accessed data and when. Can Redwood deliver logs with user principal, request id, model invoked, and resource region?
[05:25] Ethan: Yes, we emit audit events with request id, user id (if passed), model name, compute region, and action. We can stream to your SIEM through a dedicated connector or drop logs into a customer-owned bucket with server-side encryption. There is an option for signed logs for immutability.
[05:42] Rory: Signed logs — do you support append-only storage with integrity proofs?
[05:48] Priya: Not a full blockchain, but we can provide HMAC-signed log batches and versioned objects in S3 with Object Lock/Compliance mode if you configure their bucket that way. For Private deployments we can fully integrate with your logging infra so logs never leave your control.
[06:04] Marta: How about redaction? We may want request payload redaction for certain PHI fields before logs leave region.
[06:11] Ethan: We have a configurable logging pipeline that supports field-level redaction using rules. It's best-effort on hosted; for Dedicated/Private you get more precise controls. We'll share the rule spec.
[06:23] Aisha: Subprocessor question — do you have any third parties that could access encryption keys or plaintext?
[06:31] Jordan: No subprocessors should have access to plaintext if CMKs and proper grants are used. Some managed services like tracing/analytics may see metadata; they don't see request bodies if encryption-at-rest and in-transit is properly applied. We'll mark each subprocessor with the type of data they can access.
[06:48] Daniel: What about backups and KV cache replication? Could cache shards replicate across regions?
[06:54] Priya: For Dedicated we partition KV caches to region and replication is controllable. We can disable cross-region replication. For hosted, caching is global and might replicate; we avoid that for customers who request region isolation.
[07:05] Aisha: Can you walk us through a concrete flow: user in EU calls the API, where does the tokens and the user data live?
[07:12] Ethan: Sure — request arrives at edge (eu). It gets routed to the customer's pinned region in eu-west-1 where a worker pulls model weights and KV cache from region-local storage. If KMS is customer-managed, the envelope key decryption happens in eu-west-1 using your KMS. Audit events are emitted to your bucket in-region. Control plane calls for orchestrating may go to Redwood control plane unless Private is selected.
[07:38] Marta: Great. A small nit — earlier you said some telemetry goes to a US analytics subprocessor. Can that be turned off?
[07:45] Jordan: Yes, in Dedicated we can opt-out of 3rd party analytics and route telemetry to your bucket. For hosted, some product telemetry is used for ops; we can discuss a stricter telemetry profile as part of the DPA.
[07:59] Rory: About SSO/RBAC — we want SAML with SCIM provisioning and granular RBAC so that product engineers vs legal can't access audit logs.
[08:08] Priya: We support SSO via SAML and OIDC, plus SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based with fine-grained permissions; we also have token scoping at the model/route level. For Dedicated and Private you can integrate with your IdP for session control and SCIM.
[08:26] Aisha: Do tokens generated by Redwood contain scope info? We need to ensure least privilege.
[08:31] Ethan: Tokens include scope claims and are short-lived; we recommend rotating API keys and using OAuth-backed tokens for human users.
[08:38] Marta: On the SOC 2 report — does it include vendor management and subprocessors? We need evidence of your vetting.
[08:46] Jordan: Our SOC2 Type II covers vendor management at a control level; the subprocessor list documents specifics. We'll provide both.
[08:53] Daniel: On performance — any public benchmarks that show p95 with KMS in-region?
[08:58] Priya: We'll attach a small benchmark doc. We have examples showing p95 increases of ~10-20ms with envelope encryption patterns. For heavy loads we suggest pre-warming keys and using caching.
[09:12] Aisha: If we do Dedicated with CMK, what's the onboarding timeline? We have a Q2 regulatory milestone.
[09:19] Jordan: Typical Dedicated onboarding is 4-8 weeks depending on capacity and legal. KMS integration adds 1-2 weeks for key policy review and testing. Private deployments are longer.
[09:30] Marta: We may require subprocessor attestations for any vendor with >= 5% data access probability. How do you estimate those probabilities?
[09:38] Priya: We classify subprocessors by role (compute, observability, analytics) and map their access to data types. For probability we use access likelihood models — but for contract purposes we can provide categorical attestations (no-access, telemetry-only, potential-metadata).
[09:56] Rory: Can we get a runbook for incident response? We need timelines for breach notification and root cause.
[10:02] Jordan: Yes, we have an IR runbook summary that includes notification windows, forensics data and point of contact. We'll share that.
[10:08] Aisha: Two more quick items — data residency for embeddings derived from patient data, and model updates. If we send patient text and get embeddings stored, are those treated as PHI and do they leave region?
[10:20] Ethan: Embeddings are treated as derived data. We will store embeddings in-region for Dedicated/Private. For hosted, embeddings may be stored in region but could be used for model training for product improvements unless you opt-out. We have explicit controls in the DPA to opt-out of training/retention.
[10:40] Marta: For model updates — do you push model binaries from US repo to EU compute? Any code transit concerns?
[10:46] Priya: Model binaries are stored in per-region registries. For public models we mirror weights to region-local registries. We can provide attestations on where artifacts are stored and who has access.
[10:58] Daniel: A random question — do you provide VPC peering or PrivateLink connectors?
[11:03] Ethan: We support both VPC peering and PrivateLink. For Private deployments we can do direct on-prem connectors and private peering with no public egress.
[11:12] Aisha: This is useful. Can we have one follow-up technical session where Ethan walks through the KMS integration and a sample PKI flow?
[11:20] Jordan: Absolutely — we'll schedule an hour deep-dive next week. Ethan, you good to run it?
[11:24] Ethan: Yep, I'll prepare a runthrough with diagrams and a small demo of envelope encryption patterns.
[11:30] Marta: Last legal question — do you support data subject access requests? If a patient asks for deletion, how do we ensure derivative artifacts (embeddings) are removed?
[11:40] Priya: We have deletion APIs that purge the documents and can scrub derived artifacts. For embeddings we include a deletion flow that marks vectors for reindex and removal; for backups we document retention windows. We'll include specifics in the DPA.
[11:57] Jordan: Okay let's recap next steps...
[12:00] Jordan: Action items — Priya to share SOC2/ISO and subprocessor CSV; Jordan to send DPA redline; Ethan to schedule KMS deep dive and prepare benchmarks; Rory to send VPC CIDR; Maven to confirm target for Dedicated pilot.
[12:18] Aisha: Thanks all, that works. We'll review artifacts and route to procurement.
[12:23] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in Slack/email.
[12:28] (meeting ends)
topics: Dedicated vs Private for strict sovereignty
notes: Redwood to provide redlines and technical artifacts. Customer leaning toward Dedicated with CMK in eu-west-1. Legal needs subprocessor locations + SOC2/ISO to sign off. Watch for telemetry opt-out requirements.
